steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our CyberDemo paper: a framework that uses simulated human demonstrations plus data augmentation to learn real-world dexterous manipulation. Explain the data bottleneck in imitation learning, argue for collecting demos in simulation instead of on the real robot, describe the approach, and summarize the main results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Imitation learning for manipulation and the cost of demonstration data
2. Challenging in-domain real-world demos: the case for simulated demos + augmentation
3. CyberDemo: problem, framework, pipeline
4. System cost and results (real robot, generalization, ablation); release

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Imitation learning and data cost
- promising for robot manipulation; complex skills from human demo
- depends on high-quality demo data -> substantial human effort to collect
- worse for multi-finger dexterous hand: tasks complex/intricate, need highly detailed and precise demos

2. In-domain vs simulated demos
- in-domain demos = collected directly from deployment environment; common for manipulation
- general belief: best way = collect on real robot for that task; "gold standard" -> we challenge it
- claim: human demos in simulation can be better for real-world tasks
  - no real hardware needed, remote, parallel
  - simulator-only data augmentation -> better final performance
  - dataset hundreds of times larger than initial demo set
- but existing work trains in-domain policies in sim; sim2real transfer still unresolved

3. CyberDemo
- problem: use simulated human demos for real-world manipulation
- framework for robotic imitation learning from visual observations
- collect modest human demo data via teleoperation, low-cost devices, in sim
- extensive data augmentation on original demos -> broad visual + physical conditions not seen in collection -> robustness
- augmentations designed with sim2real transfer in mind
- unique curriculum learning strategy on augmented data; fine-tune with few real demos (3-minute trajectories)
- real-only policies suffer from lighting, object geometry, initial pose variation; ours handles without extra human effort

4. Results
- low-cost motion capture for teleop (RealSense camera), minimal effort (30-minute demo trajectory) -> robust policy
- vs pre-trained policies e.g. R3M fine-tuned on real demos: +35% quasi-static pick and place, +20% non-quasi-static rotate
- generalization: baselines fail on unseen objects; ours rotates novel tetra-valve and penta-valve at 42.5% though demos only tri-valve (Figure 1, second row)
- significant light disturbances (Figure 1, last column)
- ablation: augmentation + more sim demos beats equal increase in real demos
- will release code + human demo dataset

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Imitation learning is a promising approach for robot manipulation, because it lets the robot acquire complex skills from human demonstration. But how well it works depends a lot on having high-quality demonstration data, and collecting that data often needs a lot of human effort. This problem gets even bigger for manipulation with a multi-finger dexterous hand, since the tasks are complex and intricate and so the demonstrations need to be very detailed and precise.

For robot manipulation tasks, imitation learning commonly uses in-domain demonstrations, meaning data that is collected directly from the deployment environment. People generally believe that the most effective way to solve a specific task is to collect demonstrations directly on the real robot for that task. This has been treated as the gold standard, but we want to challenge it. We argue that collecting human demonstrations in simulation can give better results for real-world tasks. One reason is that it does not need real hardware and can be done remotely and in parallel. Another reason is that it can improve the final task performance by using data augmentation that is only possible in the simulator. With this we can generate a dataset that is hundreds of times larger than the initial demonstration set. However, existing studies use the generated dataset to train in-domain policies inside the simulation, and the sim2real problem of transferring the policies to the real world is still unresolved.

3. CyberDemo
- problem: use simulated human demos for real-world manipulation
- framework for imitation learning from visual observations, simulated human demos
- modest human demo data via teleoperation, low-cost devices, in sim
- extensive data augmentation -> broad visual + physical conditions not in collection -> robustness; designed for sim2real
- curriculum learning on augmented data; fine-tune with few real demos (3-minute trajectories)
- real-only policies suffer from lighting, object geometry, initial pose; ours handles without extra human effort

4. Results
- low-cost motion capture (RealSense camera), 30-minute demo trajectory -> robust policy
- vs R3M fine-tuned on real demos: +35% pick and place, +20% rotate
- novel tetra-valve and penta-valve at 42.5%, demos only tri-valve (Figure 1, second row); light disturbances (last column)
- ablation: augmentation + more sim demos beats equal increase in real demos
- release code + dataset

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Imitation learning is a promising approach for robot manipulation, because it lets the robot acquire complex skills from human demonstration. But how well it works depends a lot on having high-quality demonstration data, and collecting that data often needs a lot of human effort. This problem gets even bigger for manipulation with a multi-finger dexterous hand, since the tasks are complex and intricate and so the demonstrations need to be very detailed and precise.

For robot manipulation tasks, imitation learning commonly uses in-domain demonstrations, meaning data that is collected directly from the deployment environment. People generally believe that the most effective way to solve a specific task is to collect demonstrations directly on the real robot for that task. This has been treated as the gold standard, but we want to challenge it. We argue that collecting human demonstrations in simulation can give better results for real-world tasks. One reason is that it does not need real hardware and can be done remotely and in parallel. Another reason is that it can improve the final task performance by using data augmentation that is only possible in the simulator. With this we can generate a dataset that is hundreds of times larger than the initial demonstration set. However, existing studies use the generated dataset to train in-domain policies inside the simulation, and the sim2real problem of transferring the policies to the real world is still unresolved.

In this paper we study how to use simulated human demos for real-world robot manipulation tasks. We introduce CyberDemo, a new framework for robotic imitation learning from visual observations that uses simulated human demos. First we collect a modest amount of human demonstration data in a simulated environment by teleoperation with low-cost devices. Then CyberDemo adds extensive data augmentation to the original human demonstration. The augmented set covers a broad range of visual and physical conditions that were not seen during data collection, which makes the trained policy more robust to these variations. We also designed these augmentation techniques with the downstream sim2real transfer in mind. We use a unique curriculum learning strategy to train the policy on the augmented dataset, and then we fine-tune it with a few real-world demos (3-minute trajectories), which helps it transfer to real-world conditions. Policies trained only on real-world demonstrations may suffer from variations in lighting, object geometry and object initial pose, but our policy can handle these without needing additional human effort.

Our system uses a low-cost motion capture device for teleoperation (i.e., RealSense camera) and needs minimal human effort (i.e., a 30-minute demo trajectory), and it can learn a robust imitation learning policy. Even though it is affordable and needs little human effort, CyberDemo still gets better performance on the real robot. Compared with pre-trained policies, e.g. R3M fine-tuned on real-world demonstrations, CyberDemo gets a 35\% higher success rate for quasi-static pick and place tasks and a 20\% higher success rate for non-quasi-static rotate tasks. In the generalization test, the baseline methods struggle with objects not seen during testing, but our method can rotate novel tetra-valve and penta-valve with 42.5\% success rate, even though the human demonstrations only cover tri-valve (second row of Figure 1). Our method can also handle significant light disturbances (last column of Figure 1). In the ablation study we see that using data augmentation together with more demonstrations in the simulator gives better performance than the same increase in real-world demonstrations. We will make our code and human demonstration dataset publicly available to foster further research.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Imitation learning has been a promising approach in robot manipulation, making it possible to acquire complex skills from human demonstration. However, its effectiveness depends critically on the availability of high-quality demonstration data, which often requires substantial human effort to collect [1,2,3]. This challenge is amplified further for manipulation with a multi-finger dexterous hand, where the complexity and intricacy of the tasks require highly detailed and precise demonstrations.

In imitation learning, in-domain demonstrations, i.e., data collected directly from the deployment environment, are commonly used for robot manipulation tasks [4]. It is generally believed that the most effective way to solve a specific task is to collect demonstrations directly from the real robot on that task. This belief has been upheld as the gold standard, but we wish to challenge it. We argue that collecting human demonstrations in simulation can yield better results for real-world tasks, not only because it requires no real hardware and can be executed remotely and in parallel, but also because it can enhance final task performance through simulator-only data augmentation [5,6,7,8,9,10]. This makes it possible to generate a dataset hundreds of times larger than the initial demonstration set. However, while existing studies use the generated dataset to train in-domain policies within the simulation, the sim2real challenge of transferring policies to the real world remains unresolved.

In this paper, we study how to utilize simulated human demos for real-world robot manipulation tasks. We introduce CyberDemo, a novel framework for robotic imitation learning from visual observations that leverages simulated human demos. We first collect a modest amount of human demonstration data via teleoperation with low-cost devices in a simulated environment. CyberDemo then incorporates extensive data augmentation into the original human demonstration. The augmented set covers a broad spectrum of visual and physical conditions not encountered during data collection, which enhances the robustness of the trained policy against these variations. These augmentation techniques are also designed with downstream sim2real transfer in mind. We employ a unique curriculum learning strategy to train the policy on the augmented dataset, and then fine-tune it with a few real-world demos (3-minute trajectories), enabling effective transfer to real-world conditions. While policies trained only on real-world demonstrations may suffer from variations in lighting conditions, object geometry, and object initial pose, our policy can handle these without additional human effort.

Our system, which uses a low-cost motion capture device for teleoperation (i.e., RealSense camera) and requires minimal human effort (i.e., a 30-minute demo trajectory), can learn a robust imitation learning policy. Despite its affordability and low human effort, CyberDemo still achieves better performance on the real robot. Compared with pre-trained policies, e.g. R3M [11] fine-tuned on real-world demonstrations, CyberDemo achieves a 35\% higher success rate for quasi-static pick and place tasks and a 20\% higher success rate for non-quasi-static rotate tasks. In the generalization test, while baseline methods struggle with objects unseen during testing, our method can rotate novel tetra-valve and penta-valve with a 42.5\% success rate, even though human demonstrations only cover tri-valve (second row of Figure 1). Our method can also handle significant light disturbances (last column of Figure 1). In our ablation study, we observe that data augmentation, combined with more demonstrations in the simulator, yields better performance than an equivalent increase in real-world demonstrations. To foster further research, we will make our code and human demonstration dataset publicly available.
